slides.title: ScholarTasks
slides.narration: Hi everyone. I want to show you ScholarTasks, an app built to make the college years less stressful. It helps with college plans, scholarships, state money like Georgia's HOPE and Florida's Bright Futures, grades and test prep. It's all in one place, on the phone and on the web, in English or Spanish.

slides.title: The problem
slides.narration: Most of us have felt this. Deadlines are spread across a dozen websites. Georgia's HOPE grade point average is counted differently from the one on the report card. Scholarships are all over the internet. And our school counselors have a lot of students. ScholarTasks pulls all of this into one place.

slides.title: What it is
slides.narration: Think of it in three parts. Plan: what to do, and when. Fund: how to find and keep the money, from HOPE to private scholarships. Prepare: grades, study habits and test scores, starting as early as eighth grade.

slides.title: How it works
slides.narration: Getting started takes a few minutes. A parent signs up and adds a student. The app makes a short join code. You tap Text or Email to send it, and your student types it in on their own phone. From then on, everything the family adds lands in one shared plan.

slides.title: The family account
slides.narration: This is one of the biggest differences from other apps. The parent owns the account, and decides what each student can change. Parents also get their own space. They can search colleges and scholarships, keep their own lists and notes, look over the career quiz, and share the ideas they like, without any of it showing up as the student's work. Every permission, approval and signed consent is in one place there too, and a separate My students page shows how each child is doing. The student has their own app, and does the day to day work. When a student turns eighteen, they get a say in what parents can still see.

slides.title: AI counselor
slides.narration: The AI counselor is like having a college counselor on call. It can see the student's grades, college list and deadlines, so its answers are about your child, not general advice. It will explain and coach, but it won't do homework or write essays. And it's advice only. Your family makes the decisions.

slides.title: Scholarships
slides.narration: Instead of searching a dozen websites, students answer a few questions. Then they see awards sorted into You qualify, Maybe, and Not a fit. There are hundreds of Georgia and national awards, and the list grows every week. Each new award is checked on its official page before families see it, and re-checked twice a week in scholarship season. Then students apply step by step, right in the app. Each award gets its own page with the questions on the form, the papers and recommendation letters it needs, and a bar that shows what to do next. Short answers they already wrote show up as a starting point, and a copy-ready profile fills in the rest. For your school's own local scholarships, students send the application to the counselor right inside the app. And the app keeps track of what was sent and what was won.

slides.title: Essay challenge
slides.narration: From time to time, ScholarTasks runs an essay challenge for each grade group, with a fresh topic in a different subject, like science, history or careers. Students write right in the app, step by step, like a game. They jot ideas, make a plan, write a draft, come back another day to improve it, and polish it, earning a badge for each step. Pasting is turned off, and the coach gives tips but never writes, so every word is their own. A parent signs permission in the app. Our review team judges with names hidden, so free and paid accounts have the same chance. Every student who finishes gets a certificate, and winners win gift cards that a parent picks up safely in the app.

slides.title: Grades 8 to 12
slides.narration: HOPE is earned in high school, so starting early matters. From eighth grade on, the scorecard shows the HOPE grade point average next to the school one, so there are no surprises later. If a grade slips, Grade Rescue asks a few questions and builds a simple plan. A four-year course plan adds up graduation credits and the rigor courses HOPE needs, and the AI suggests where to stretch.

slides.title: Strong study habits
slides.narration: Good grades come from good habits, and those start in middle school. ScholarTasks teaches students how to study, lets them test themselves, and gives them a tutor that explains instead of handing over answers. Families set goals together, Grade Rescue catches a slipping grade early, and course advice helps students take harder classes at the right pace.

slides.title: Homework Helper
slides.narration: Kids today can copy and paste an answer in seconds, and they learn nothing. The Homework Helper is the safe alternative. It helps with any subject, from algebra to essays, but it never gives the answer and never writes for the student. Students can type the problem, or just say it out loud. Every AI helper in the app has a Speak button, so explaining their reasoning takes seconds, and the words appear for them to check before sending. They can also snap a photo of their work, or upload the assignment. It asks what they tried, gives one hint at a time, finds the first mistake in their work, and asks them to explain their thinking. A second AI checks every reply before the student sees it. Students can save a one-page study sheet of each session and reopen recent problems. Parents see what was practiced, how many hints it took, and every time the helper said no. And every Monday, parents get a short progress email. When the numbers show real progress, it says exactly what improved. When they don't, it suggests one different thing to try at home that week. The goal is a student who can think it through on their own, even with the phone switched off.

slides.title: Beyond grades
slides.narration: Colleges and scholarships also look at activities, leadership, service and recommendation letters. Each school year, ScholarTasks adds the right milestones for that grade to the to-do list. Students log service hours and activities as they go, keep track of who will write their letters, and build a brag sheet for teachers. A quick check-up shows what is already strong and what to work on next, so senior year is not a scramble.

slides.title: Study and test prep
slides.narration: Test prep is built in. There are over six hundred original practice questions for the SAT and the ACT, plus timed practice tests and a score plan. The study library teaches how to study. Our education review team checks the content. These are our own questions, not copies of real tests.

slides.title: Colleges
slides.narration: Students can search more than five thousand colleges, choose public, private or Christian colleges, even by church family, take a quick match quiz, and add a school with one tap. Each college is marked reach, match or likely, based on grades, harder classes and test scores, and shows an estimated cost after state aid and saved scholarships. The essay coach gives feedback on a draft typed in, uploaded from Word, or photographed from paper, and the draft downloads back as a Word file. It never writes for the student. And the Common App ready page checks every activity, honor and essay against Common App's limits, so applying is just copy, paste and submit.

slides.title: Search by major
slides.narration: Most students know what they love before they know where to go. Type in a dream, like marine biology, vet or nursing. You'll see what those careers earn, and how many years of school they take. Then you get the strongest programs in your own state first, and across the whole country too, with a yearly cost for your family. Then compare your favorites side by side. Each college is ranked first, second or third on strength in the major, cost, graduation, pay and debt, in your state and nationwide, and you choose what matters most. It even shows what you could save by starting at a two-year college, then transferring. Not sure yet? Start with the career interest quiz: more than a hundred questions about what a student likes to do and what matters to them in a job, drawn fresh from a bank of six hundred, so no two friends get the same quiz. If the top interests are close, a short second round narrows it down. It suggests college careers, skilled trades and military paths. It measures interests, not intelligence, and never uses race or gender.

slides.title: Trades and careers
slides.narration: Not every student wants a four-year degree, and many great careers start with a trade. ScholarTasks covers sixty-seven skilled trades, with what each one earns, how long training takes, and what license is needed. That includes well-paid careers many families have never heard of, like CNC machining, power plant operator, ultrasound technician and air traffic controller. Students can find training near home or anywhere in the country, follow step by step apply checklists, and see ways to fund it, like Georgia's HOPE Grant. And companies anywhere in the country can post apprenticeships, paid training and trade internships for free. Students see openings near home first. Our team checks every listing, nothing about the student is shared, and students choose who to contact, then keep track of each application in the app with a parent's OK, so it opens doors for small businesses and for students who want to start working and learning right away. Weekend and holiday jobs have their own place, with their own teen job rules. Students apply right in the app, and nothing reaches the company until a parent reads it and taps I agree, with every consent kept in a permanent record. A job they get goes on their activities and resume in one tap, and if the company writes a reference letter, the parent decides whether it goes in the student's records.

slides.title: Military paths
slides.narration: Some students want to serve their country, and the military can pay for college too. ScholarTasks compares the four ways in: a service academy like West Point or the Naval Academy, an ROTC scholarship at a regular college, a military college like the University of North Georgia, or enlisting with paid job training. It explains how to get a nomination from your senators and representative, puts every step from junior year on the to-do list, and shows the GI Bill and other ways service helps fund school. Families can also pick military academies and colleges in the college search.

slides.title: FAFSA and state aid
slides.narration: Aid forms scare a lot of families. ScholarTasks breaks the FAFSA and your own state's forms into small steps, and explains who does each part. It covers Georgia and ten more Southeast states, from Florida's Bright Futures to Louisiana's TOPS, and links every other state to its aid office. You still file on the official government sites. We never ask for or keep FSA IDs, Social Security numbers or tax returns. When award letters arrive, type them in, and compare free money, loans and the real price, side by side.

slides.title: To-do list
slides.narration: Everything with a date lands on one to-do list, already sorted into late, due this week, and coming up. Email reminders go out a month before, then two weeks, one week, two days and one day before. Dates can show up in your own calendar, and the phone app can remind the student too. Reminders come in English or Spanish, whichever the family reads the app in.

slides.title: Phone app
slides.narration: Families live on their phones, so ScholarTasks does too. The iPhone and Android apps are in testing now, and the website works on any device. Sign-in is quick with Face ID or a fingerprint, which helps, because teenagers forget passwords. Remember me keeps you signed in at home, and on a shared computer you just untick it. What you add on the phone shows up on the computer too. The menu stays short: only the headings show until you tap one, and every page links back to its section.

slides.title: Grade 8 to graduation
slides.narration: Here's how a family uses it over the years. In sixth and seventh grade, a parent and student start with study habits and the career quiz. In eighth and ninth grade, it's the scorecard, study skills and choosing courses. Tenth grade adds HOPE tracking, harder classes, and exploring majors and trades. Eleventh grade is test prep and the college list. Senior year is applications, scholarships and aid forms. Week to week, it takes a few minutes.

slides.title: How we compare 1
slides.narration: Here's how we compare on planning and funding college. Other apps do one or two of these things well. ScholarTasks is the only one we found that links parent and student, has an AI counselor that knows your state, tracks HOPE and Zell Miller, and walks you through the FAFSA, all in one place.

slides.title: How we compare 2
slides.narration: On grades, test prep and trust, the picture is the same. No other app we found coaches grades and course choices from eighth grade. Reminders come by email, text, calendar and phone. Our school portal is free for every school. And we will never sell student data.

slides.title: How we compare 3
slides.narration: This fall we added the things other apps still did better. A four-year course plan that checks HOPE's harder-class rule. Reach, match and likely based on grades and harder classes, not just test scores. A homework helper that never gives answers. Side-by-side aid offers. The whole app in Spanish, reminders and AI answers too. Parent-managed accounts from sixth grade. Roster upload for schools. And now, applying to scholarships right inside the app. In our latest check, ScholarTasks covers more of the list than any other app.

slides.title: Why we are better
slides.narration: If you remember one slide, make it this one. ScholarTasks puts your state first, but shows options in every state. It's built for families, and it covers every path, from a four-year degree to a skilled trade. It keeps everything in one place, uses AI honestly, and never sells your child's data. It's built in Georgia, and our review team checks every lesson and question before families see it.

slides.title: Safety and privacy
slides.narration: Parents always ask about privacy, and they should. We never sell data, and we never ask for the most sensitive numbers. Students sign in at thirteen and up, and parents manage younger students, with no AI. Every family's information is kept separate. Students agree before using AI help. When a parent gives consent, they sign with a finger and confirm it's really them with Face ID or an email code, so a child can't agree in their place. And you can delete everything from inside the app.

slides.title: For schools
slides.narration: For school leaders and counselors: ScholarTasks supports your counselors. It doesn't replace them. Our school portal is free for every school. Counselors can see who filed the FAFSA, who has a college list, and who's behind on deadlines. They can upload a class roster to see who has joined, email a whole grade at once, and post local scholarships just for their families. Students apply for those right in the app, and counselors mark each one awarded or not. Families choose what to share with a school code, and can stop any time. Essays, AI chats and income are never shared, unless a student chooses to send an essay with an application for the school's own scholarship.

slides.title: What it costs
slides.narration: Families can start for free, with no credit card. The paid family plan covers every child in the house, and it will cost less than most paid apps for test prep or essays. We're setting final prices now, so I won't quote a number today. But it will be affordable.

slides.title: Questions?
slides.narration: Thank you. Everything you saw today is on our website, scholartasks dot com, with a page for schools, a comparison with other apps, this tour, and a contact form. Start as a parent, add your student, and send them the join code. If you get stuck, the help guide walks through every page, or email us at support at scholartasks dot com. And if you like it, tap Invite a friend in the menu to text it to another family in one tap, or tap Rate ScholarTasks to tell us how we're doing. I'm happy to take questions.
